Deceitfully
de-SEET-ful-lee
adverb
From the Old French deceite, and that from the Latin decipere, to take in, to catch as in a snare — de, down, and capere, to take. It renders the Hebrew mirmah, fraud, and remiyyah, slackness or treachery.

Biblical Definition

To act deceitfully is to take a man as a hunter takes a bird — by a snare he cannot see. Scripture traces the sin through every department of life. In the family it appears at Shechem, where the sons of Jacob “answered Shechem and Hamor his father deceitfully” (Gen 34:13), covering murder with the language of covenant and circumcision — religion itself made the bait. In business it is the false weight and the withheld wage, the thing “which he hath deceitfully gotten” (Lev 6:4), which the law requires be restored with a fifth part added. In worship it is the great disqualifier: he that shall ascend into the hill of the LORD is the man with clean hands and a pure heart, “who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully” (Psa 24:4). And most solemnly it appears in the ministry, where Paul disclaims “handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2) — the phrase means adulterating it as a huckster waters wine, and the alternative he names is manifestation of the truth. Job cuts to the root when he asks the comforters, “will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?” (Job 13:7). Men will lie on God’s behalf and call it defending Him. He needs no such defenders.

Webster 1828 Definition

In a manner intended to mislead; fraudulently; by snare or false appearance. Applied in Scripture to speech, to trade, to oaths, and above all to the handling of God’s word.

expand to see more

DECEITFULLY, adv. In a deceitful manner; fraudulently; with intent to mislead.

From deceit; Old French deceite; Latin decipere, to ensnare, from de and capere, to take.

In trade, by false weights, false measures, or concealed defects (Lev 6:4).

In oath-taking, to swear with a reserved or contrary intention (Psa 24:4).

In teaching, to adulterate or corrupt a text for advantage (2Co 4:2).

Key Scripture

Gen 34:13 — "And the sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father deceitfully, and said, because he had defiled Dinah their sister:"

Job 13:7 — "Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?"

Psa 24:4 — "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully."

2Co 4:2 — "But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God."

Modern Corruption

Deceit has been rebranded as skill — spin, positioning, curation, managing the narrative — so that the same act which Scripture calls a snare is now taught as competence.

expand to see more

The corruption is euphemism. No one advertises deceit, so it travels under professional names: the advertisement positions, the spokesman frames, the applicant optimises his history, the believer curates the version of his life that others see. Each word grants permission to create an impression the speaker knows to be false while keeping every individual sentence technically defensible, and that is precisely the sin Scripture names. The Hebrew mirmah does not require a stated falsehood; it requires a snare. Jacob’s sons at Shechem told no outright lie — they proposed circumcision, a genuine covenant sign — and used it as a trap. The most dangerous deceit has always dressed in true statements and religious clothing.

Recover the plain sense: measure speech not by whether each clause can be defended but by what impression it was designed to leave. Psa 24:4 sets the standard at the sanctuary door — clean hands, a pure heart, and no oath sworn deceitfully — and 2Co 4:2 sets it in the pulpit, where the only lawful method is manifestation of the truth. Job 13:7 closes the last loophole, the pious lie told to protect God’s reputation. A cause that requires deceit to advance it is not His cause, and a man who will shade the truth for God will soon shade it for himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin decipere, to take in a snare — the sin of creating a false impression, whether by lie, by silence, or by true words falsely aimed.

expand to see more

Deceitfully — Latin de + capere, to take down, to ensnare.

Hebrew mirmah, fraud, treachery (Gen 34:13; Psa 24:4).

The image is the fowler’s snare, not merely the spoken lie.

2Co 4:2 opposes it to manifestation of the truth — the minister’s only method.

Job 13:7 forbids the pious falsehood told on God’s behalf.

Usage

"Gen 34:13: a true covenant sign used as bait — deceit needs no stated lie."

"Psa 24:4 makes truthful swearing a condition of approach to God."

"2Co 4:2 condemns adulterating the word as a huckster waters his wine."
